label: Anatomy of an Argument
chapter: CHAPTER I — THE ANATOMY OF AN ARGUMENT
oneLiner: Every argument is premises offered in support of a conclusion; everything else is context or counterpoint.
definition: An argument is a set of claims in which some (premises) are offered as reasons to accept another (the conclusion). Background context sets the stage; counterpoints are views the author argues against. Diagramming the roles of each sentence is the first move on nearly every LR question.
objectives: Label every sentence of a stimulus as conclusion, premise, sub-conclusion, context, or counterpoint
Use the “Why?” test to confirm which claim is the conclusion
Recognize premise and conclusion indicator words

examples.text: “The café will be packed—it’s Saturday and the band is playing.” Conclusion: packed. Premises: Saturday; band playing.
“The statute does not apply to the defendant, since it covers only residents and the defendant lives abroad.” Conclusion first, premises after “since.”
“Analysts expect the bond to be downgraded; the issuer missed two payments. But the issuer has secured new financing, so a downgrade is unlikely.” Counterpoint, then the author’s conclusion.

attack: Read the whole stimulus once for gist
Find the claim the author wants you to believe (conclusion)
Apply the Why? test: each premise answers “why believe that?”
Mark counterpoints (views the author rejects) and context
Note any claim that is both supported and supporting (sub-conclusion)
correctLooksLike: A diagram in which every premise points (directly or through a sub-conclusion) to exactly one main conclusion.
traps: Taking the last sentence as the conclusion by default
Mistaking a counterpoint for the author’s view
Treating a sub-conclusion as the main conclusion
commonError: Assuming the conclusion comes last. Conclusions often appear first or in the middle, followed by “since/because.”

keyPoints.point: The conclusion is the claim the premises support
Premises are reasons; apply the Why? test
Counterpoints are opposing views the author rebuts
A sub-conclusion is both supported and supporting

card.front: Name the five roles a sentence can play in an LR stimulus.
card.back: Main conclusion, premise, sub-(intermediate) conclusion, counterpoint (opposing view), context/background.

label: Identify the Question Type
oneLiner: The stem tells you your task; classify it before you read the stimulus closely.
definition: Each LR question type has signature stem language. Classifying the stem first tells you whether to read the stimulus as an argument to critique, a set of facts to combine, or a structure to describe.
objectives: Classify any LR stem into one of 19 types in under 5 seconds
Know which types treat the stimulus as true and which attack it

examples.text: A recipe card says “serves four”: you know the task (portioning) before you cook.
“The argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that…” → Flaw.
“Which one of the following, if true, most helps to resolve the apparent discrepancy…” → Paradox.

attack: Read the stem first
Spot the action verb: must be true / weakens / assumes / resolves / most similar
Note “if true” (you may add info) vs. “if the statements above are true” (stimulus proves)
Note EXCEPT and reverse the task
Decide how you will read the stimulus
correctLooksLike: A one-word label (“NA”, “Weaken”, “MBT”) written before you read the stimulus.
traps: Confusing Necessary and Sufficient Assumption stems
commonError: Mixing up “assumption required by” (Necessary) with “conclusion follows logically if assumed” (Sufficient).

keyPoints.point: Read the stem before the stimulus
“If true” answers may add new information

card.front: “The argument relies on the assumption that…” — which type?
card.back: Necessary Assumption: the answer must be true for the argument to work (apply the Negation Test).

label: Timing & Section Management
oneLiner: Average ~1:20 per LR question and ~8:30 per RC set; skip early, return later.
definition: A 35-minute LR section with ~25 questions leaves about 84 seconds each, but early questions are usually faster. Elite scorers bank time on easy questions, flag time-sinks after ~2 minutes, and use a second pass on flagged items.
objectives: Hold a 1:20 LR average with a deliberate skip policy
Run a two-pass section
Recognize your personal time-sinks from analytics

examples.text: At a museum with an hour left, you see the highlights first and return to rooms you skipped.
A litigator triages motions: dispositive issues first, minor ones later.
A portfolio manager cuts a losing position at a preset stop-loss rather than “waiting it out.”

attack: Pass 1: answer what you can in ≤ 2:00; flag and move on otherwise
Note your checkpoint (~question 10 by 10:00, 20 by 23:00)
Pass 2: return to flagged questions in order of promise
Never leave an answer blank—there is no guessing penalty
Use blind review afterward to learn from flags
correctLooksLike: A section where no single question consumed more than ~2:30 and every question has an answer.
traps: Sunk-cost thinking on a hard question
commonError: Spending four minutes on question 14 and losing three easier questions at the end.

keyPoints.point: About 1:20 per LR question on average
Flag and move on after about two minutes

card.front: What is the target average pace for LR questions?
card.back: About 1 minute 20 seconds per question (~25 questions in 35 minutes), with a flag-and-return policy after ~2 minutes.

label: The Wrong-Answer Taxonomy
oneLiner: Name why each wrong answer is wrong; there are only about ten recurring reasons.
definition: LSAT wrong answers recur in recognizable patterns: Out of Scope, Too Strong, Reversal, Half-Right/Half-Wrong, Irrelevant Comparison, Opposite, Shell Game, Unsupported Inference, Wrong Degree, and Restatement of Premise. Labeling each eliminated answer builds speed and turns guessing into diagnosis.
objectives: Label any wrong answer with its trap
Use elimination as a second path to the right answer
Recognize which traps tempt you most (from your Ledger)

examples.text: A witness who says “definitely” about something they glimpsed is Too Strong.
A brief that answers a question the court did not ask is Out of Scope.
An analyst who says profits rose because revenue rose, ignoring costs, is offering a Half-Right story.

attack: Predict an answer first
Eliminate obvious misfits with a label
Compare the final two on the exact words
Choose the answer that fits the task, not the one that “sounds smart”
correctLooksLike: Four labels for four wrong answers, and one answer that survives scrutiny word for word.
traps: Choosing an answer because it is true in the real world
Falling for strong language in inference questions
Picking the answer that restates a premise on assumption questions
commonError: Eliminating the right answer because of an unfamiliar word, while keeping a familiar-sounding wrong one.

keyPoints.point: Out of Scope introduces new topics
Half-right answers fail on one part
Shell Game swaps a key term

card.front: An answer says “All X are Y” when the stimulus said “most”. Trap?
card.back: Too Strong (or Wrong Degree): it overstates what the evidence supports.

label: Blind Review
oneLiner: Before seeing answers, re-do flagged questions untimed with written justifications; compare timed vs. blind scores.
definition: Blind review separates understanding problems from timing problems. If your blind-review score is high but your timed score is low, the issue is speed or nerves; if both are low, the issue is understanding.
objectives: Run blind review on every practice test
Interpret the gap between timed and blind scores
Write justifications that would persuade a skeptical reader

examples.text: Re-reading an email you drafted in a rush—before sending—catches errors you could have caught with time.
Appellate review: the court reconsiders the record without the pressure of trial.
A post-mortem on a trade made under deadline, conducted before you check the P&L.

attack: Flag uncertain questions during the test
Before checking answers, re-answer flagged ones untimed
Write a one-paragraph justification for each
Score both versions
Diagnose: timing gap vs. understanding gap
correctLooksLike: Two scores (timed, blind) and a list of the questions that changed—with a reason for each.
commonError: Only reviewing questions you got wrong; lucky guesses hide gaps that will cost you later.

keyPoints.point: Big gap = timing problem; both low = understanding problem

card.front: Timed score 160, blind review 172. What does the gap suggest?
card.back: Mostly a timing/pressure problem—your understanding is ahead of your speed.

label: Test-Day Readiness
oneLiner: Routine, rest, and a rehearsed plan beat last-minute cramming.
definition: Performance on test day depends on sleep, routine, logistics, and a pre-committed plan for difficult moments. The last week is for maintenance, not new learning.
objectives: Rehearse your test-day routine
Prepare a reset ritual for a bad section
Taper volume in the final week

examples.text: A marathoner tapers mileage before race day.
Counsel prepares an opening statement and then rests the night before trial.
A deal team freezes the model before signing and stops tinkering.

attack: Simulate start time for two weeks
Taper the final 5 days
Prepare logistics (ID, check-in, equipment)
Use a 3-breath reset between sections
Treat the experimental section as scored
correctLooksLike: A calm, routine morning and a section-by-section plan you have already practiced.
traps: Judging how you are doing mid-test
commonError: Trying to guess which section is experimental and coasting through it.

keyPoints.point: Rehearse the routine at test time

card.front: Should you try to identify the experimental section?
card.back: No. Treat every section as scored; guessing wrong costs points.

label: The Writing Format
oneLiner: A debatable issue with several perspectives; prewrite (15 min), then write a persuasive essay (35 min).
definition: LSAT Argumentative Writing presents a debatable issue and several perspectives. You analyze the perspectives in a guided prewriting stage, then take and defend a position, engaging at least one perspective. It is unscored but sent to every school.
objectives: Know the timing and structure of the task
State a clear position in your first paragraph
Engage counterarguments explicitly

examples.text: Writing a letter to a landlord arguing for a repair, anticipating the landlord’s objections.
A short bench memo recommending a ruling and addressing the strongest contrary argument.
An investment memo that recommends a position and rebuts the bear case.

attack: Read the issue and every perspective
Map positions and tensions (prewriting)
Choose a defensible thesis
Plan: thesis → reasons → counterargument → response → conclusion
Write cleanly; reserve 3 minutes to proofread
correctLooksLike: A clear thesis, organized reasons, honest engagement with a competing perspective, and precise prose.
commonError: Spending the essay summarizing the perspectives instead of taking and defending a position.

card.front: What must every Argumentative Writing essay do?
card.back: Take a clear position on the issue and engage at least one of the given perspectives.

label: Visual Prewriting
oneLiner: Map your position, the perspectives, and their tensions before you write a sentence.
definition: A short visual pre-write—position at the center, perspectives around it, supports and objections linked—turns a blank page into an outline and prevents the most common essay failure: drifting without a thesis.
objectives: Build a prewrite map in under 10 minutes
Convert the map into a 5-paragraph plan

examples.text: Sketching a floor plan before moving furniture.
Drawing an issue tree before drafting a brief.
Building a decision tree before an investment committee meeting.

attack: Put your tentative position at the center
Add each perspective as a node
Link supports (green) and objections (red)
Pick the strongest objection to answer
Number the nodes into an outline
correctLooksLike: A map with one central position, every perspective connected, and a numbered path through it.
traps: Over-elaborate maps that eat writing time
commonError: Spending the whole prewriting period on an elaborate map and running out of writing time.

keyPoints.point: Turn the map into an outline

card.front: What sits at the center of a prewrite map?

label: Thesis & Structure
oneLiner: A precise, arguable thesis followed by reasons in a deliberate order.
definition: A strong thesis is specific, arguable, and appropriately qualified. Structure follows from it: strongest reasons first, then the counterargument and your response.

card.front: Three properties of a strong thesis?

label: Engaging Perspectives
oneLiner: State the opposing view at its strongest, then answer it.
definition: Engagement means steelmanning: representing a perspective fairly before explaining why your position survives it.

card.front: What does it mean to “steelman” a perspective?
card.back: Represent it at its strongest before responding.
